opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think convolutions are actually really interesting and somewhat underrated as an approach to sequence modeling, including language. There's a long history there. People tried CNNs for language well before transformers took over, things like ByteNet and gated convolutional networks from Facebook, and they were reasonably competitive at the time. But the standard local convolutions have a fundamental limitation, which is that the receptive field is limited by the kernel size. To capture long-range context you need to stack a lot of layers or use dilations, and that's never felt fully natural for language, where you might need to reference something from thousands of tokens back.

What's changed more recently, and this connects to a lot of my own work on state space models, is the idea of long convolutions, where the kernel is as long as the sequence itself. An S4 model, for instance, can be computed as a convolution with a very long, implicitly parameterized kernel. Models like Hyena build on that same idea. They use FFTs, so the cost is closer to N log N than the quadratic cost of attention. That gives you a global receptive field while staying efficient.

That said, I'd be honest that for language specifically, pure convolutional models have had a harder time than in other modalities. On audio, genomics, and other continuous or very long signals, long convolutions and SSMs do really well, sometimes better than transformers. Language is different. It's discrete and very information-dense, and a lot of what you need is content-dependent reasoning: looking up a specific token or copying something based on what it is, not just where it is. A convolution is fundamentally linear time-invariant. It applies the same filter regardless of the input, and that's exactly where it struggles on things like associative recall.

A lot of the progress has come from recognizing that limitation and adding input dependence. That's part of the motivation behind selectivity in Mamba. Once you make the dynamics depend on the input, you lose the convolutional view, so you can't use the FFT trick anymore and need different algorithms, like parallel scans, to stay efficient. In some sense the field has moved from convolutions toward recurrent models that are more expressive, while keeping the efficiency people liked about convolutions.

So my overall assessment is that convolutions are an important building block and a really useful lens for understanding these models. Short convolutions in particular still show up in a lot of modern architectures, including Mamba, as a cheap way to mix local information. But as the primary mechanism for language modeling, I think you need something more than pure time-invariant convolution to match transformers on the things that matter most for language.

r001.rationale: The candidate says pure time-invariant convolution is insufficient as the primary language-modeling mechanism, but does not characterize convolutional architectures as fundamentally unsuitable; it also describes them as useful building blocks.

r002.rationale: It says long convolutions and SSMs work well on audio, genomics, and other continuous or very long signals, but does not identify high-resolution data as particularly well suited.

r003.rationale: It describes S4 as computable by long convolution and mentions FFT efficiency, but does not explain that recurrent models were reformulated as convolutions to address their computational inefficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because a lot of my own work kind of sits right at that boundary. If you look at a model like S4, or the structured state space models that came before Mamba, one way to view them is literally as long convolutions. The state space formulation is one thing, but when you actually compute them in training mode, you're just computing a global convolution over the whole sequence with a very particular, structured kernel. So in a sense I've been building convolutional language models for years, even if we didn't always call them that.

And I think the honest assessment is that convolutions get you surprisingly far. They're efficient, they parallelize beautifully, you get this nice sub-quadratic scaling in sequence length, and on a lot of benchmarks, especially things like the Long Range Arena at the time, they just dominated. Work like Hyena pushed this further and showed you could get pretty competitive perplexity on real language data with essentially no attention at all. So the ceiling is higher than people initially assumed.

But where I've landed is that there's a fundamental limitation, and it's basically that a convolution is a linear time-invariant system. The kernel is fixed. It doesn't depend on the input. So the model has to decide ahead of time, at the parameter level, how it's going to mix information across time, and it can't change that based on what it's actually reading. For a lot of signal processing style data, like audio, that's totally fine, and it's actually a great inductive bias. But language is really the opposite of that. The information content is extremely discrete and context dependent. Whether a token matters depends entirely on what came before it, and you want the model to be able to selectively remember some things and ignore others.

That's really what motivated the move to selective state spaces in Mamba. The whole point was to make the dynamics input-dependent, which means you lose the convolutional view, because you can no longer express it as a single fixed kernel. You have to go back to the recurrent formulation and be clever about hardware to make it fast. But that selectivity is what closes a lot of the gap on things like in-context learning, associative recall, copying, these synthetic tasks that turn out to be really predictive of language modeling quality.

So my overall take is that convolutions are a great building block, and they're a clean lens for understanding a lot of these sequence models. But as the sole mechanism for language, I think they hit a wall, because language needs some form of content-based selection. Whether you get that from attention, or from selective recurrence, or from some hybrid, I think that's the real design space. Pure convolution, in my view, is not where language modeling ends up.

r001.rationale: It says pure convolution has a fundamental limitation for language and that content-based selection is needed, so convolution alone is insufficient for language modeling.

r002.rationale: It says convolution is a good fit for signal-processing-style data such as audio, but does not identify continuous, high-resolution data as particularly well suited.

r003.rationale: It describes S4 models as long convolutions, but does not say recurrent models were reformulated as convolutions to address their computational inefficiency.

astra-6.text:
I think convolutions have some appealing properties for language modeling. You can train them in parallel, and they give you a natural way to capture local patterns. The challenge is that language also requires long-range dependencies. With a standard convolution, you have a fixed window, so you need to stack layers or use dilation to expand how much context the model can see.

But I think it’s useful to distinguish those standard, short convolutions from long convolutions that can span the entire sequence. State space models, for example, can be expressed as a kind of long convolution during training, while also having a recurrent form that’s convenient for generation. So I wouldn’t dismiss convolution as an approach. A lot depends on how you parameterize it and whether you can efficiently capture the dependencies that matter for language.

r001.rationale: The response says convolution should not be dismissed and that suitability depends on parameterization and capturing dependencies; it does not call convolution fundamentally unsuitable for standard language modeling.

r002.rationale: The response mentions local patterns and long-range dependencies, but does not identify continuous, high-resolution data as particularly well suited to convolutional models.

r003.rationale: It says state space models can be expressed as long convolutions during training, but does not explain that recurrent models were reformulated as convolutions to overcome their computational inefficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think convolutions are an interesting approach, because they give you a different set of trade-offs from attention. During training, you can apply a convolution across a whole sequence in parallel, and the operation has a very clear interpretation: you’re combining information from different positions using a shared filter.

The challenge for language is that the information you need depends on the input. A fixed convolutional filter doesn’t directly give you the kind of content-dependent lookup that attention does. And with a conventional short convolution, you need to stack layers or use dilation to communicate over long distances.

One of the motivations for our work on state space models is that you can get a very long convolution, with a structured way of parameterizing that filter. You can also view the same computation as a recurrence, which is useful when you’re generating tokens one at a time.

So I think convolution is a useful computational primitive. The bigger question is how you build a model around it that can both remember information over long sequences and selectively use the information that matters for the next prediction.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls convolution a useful computational primitive and discusses trade-offs and limitations, but does not judge convolutional architectures fundamentally unsuitable for standard language modeling.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention continuous, high-resolution data or identify it as particularly suited to convolution.

r003.rationale: The candidate says state space models can be viewed as long convolutions and recurrences, but does not explain that Gu reformulated recurrent models as convolutions to address their computational inefficiency.
